itineraries.title: Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days
itineraries.subtitle: Over 20 days starting in Faro, you travel between the Algarve’s lagoons, Andalusian cities, and Alentejo villages.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary is packed: choose optional activities to suit your pace. Book the Alhambra and check with your rental company that you are allowed to drive between Portugal and Spain.
itineraries.climate: Favor April–May and October: in Seville, average highs are around 23 to 27 °C, according to AEMET. Avoid July–August for city sightseeing, when average highs in Seville are close to 35 to 36 °C. Bring a windproof layer for the Atlantic capes and adjust sea outings to local conditions.

visits.text: Behind the ramparts, the noise of Faro suddenly fades. The Cidade Velha has cobblestone lanes and squares that turn their backs on the marina; this contrast alone gets your loop underway. Leave your car outside the neighborhood and favor the narrow, shaded streets for this first walk.

Head up to the Sé de Faro to get a better sense of the landscape. From its bell tower, the old town’s rooftops give way to the channels of Ria Formosa; the lagoon is easier to understand from here than from the waterfront. Climb the bell tower in shoes with good traction and locate the channels on the lagoon side before heading back down.

activities.text: If sea conditions and schedules allow, Ria Formosa is worth a boat trip. The barrier islands separate the channels from the ocean: the landscape changes with the tide, without requiring a long voyage. Choose a departure from Faro and confirm your return before continuing to Tavira.

practical_info.tip: Optional outing: choose it in place of a city visit if you arrive late.

visits.text: The Castelo de Tavira offers a green retreat above the rooftops. Its walls now surround a garden rather than a furnished palace: the main reason to visit is the view of the town and lagoon. Head up before the hottest hours and take care on the steps and sections of rampart.

Roman in name, but more complicated in its history: the Ponte Romana crosses the Gilão in Tavira. Its common name does not prove that it was built in antiquity; the bridge has undergone several reconstructions. Walk across between the two banks and view it from the waterfront, where its arches are easier to make out.

activities.text: You can replace a city visit with the crossing to Ilha de Tavira. The island is part of Ria Formosa’s system of sand barriers: between the landing dock and the ocean, the landscape truly changes. Buy a round-trip ticket before boarding and make this crossing a substitute for an extended visit to the town center.

practical_info.tip: Beach option: do not combine the crossing with all the visits planned for this half-day.

visits.text: The best of the Fortaleza de Cacela Velha is seen from outside. Its bastions overlook the lagoon beside the village’s small whitewashed center; focus on the panorama from the area around the fortress. Walk around the public spaces, then set aside a moment to observe the sandbars.

activities.text: If crossings are operating, head to Praia da Fábrica from the Fábrica area. The beach lies on the ocean side of a sand barrier, separated from the village by the lagoon’s channels, so access depends on water conditions. Ask locally and do not attempt to wade across a deep channel.

practical_info.tip: Adjust this option to the tides and the time available; a crossing on foot is not guaranteed.

visits.text: Sand replaces paving underfoot around the Ermita del Rocío. The shrine forms the center of a community shaped by pilgrimage, with broad streets suited to horses. Enter quietly if the church is open, and avoid timing this brief stop to coincide with a major celebration.

The Plaza del Acebuchal offers a different sense of scale in El Rocío, defined more by greenery than monuments. Its name refers to the wild olive trees in the square: a simple stop after the shrine. Stay on the public paths and enjoy the trees’ shade before getting back on the road to Seville.

activities.text: Walk along the Paseo Marismeño to look for birds without entering the protected areas. This marsh edge offers a window onto Doñana, but water conditions and the species you can see vary with the season. Bring binoculars and check access; this short walk replaces a long guided excursion.

practical_info.tip: Wildlife sightings depend on the season and water level; no animal sightings are guaranteed.

visits.text: Give the Real Alcázar de Sevilla enough time instead of fitting in a quick stop between two ticketed visits. The courtyards, the decoration of Pedro I’s palace, and the gardens offer different experiences, with Mudéjar art that challenges simplistic distinctions between cultures. The complex is part of the property inscribed by UNESCO in 1987 alongside the cathedral and the Archive of the Indies. Book on the official website and allow extra time before your entry slot.

A former minaret turned bell tower, the Giralda offers a key to understanding the Catedral de Sevilla. Inside, the soaring vaults and the great altarpiece shift the scale of the visit again. The Patio de los Naranjos also preserves traces of the earlier religious complex. Book your cathedral–Giralda ticket before your stay, then climb the tower at the beginning of your visit.

Explore the Plaza de España by following its galleries instead of staying in the center. The ceramic benches represent Spain’s provinces; looking for their scenes gives you a reason to slow down in front of the sweeping monumental arc. The square connects directly to the Parque de María Luisa. Come early for the light and shade, then take your time around the pool and footbridges.

The Torre del Oro provides a compact landmark between the Guadalquivir and Seville’s major monuments. Its polygonal shape is easier to appreciate from the waterfront than in a tightly framed photograph; an interior visit adds maritime context when the rooms are accessible. First compare the views from the riverbank, then check the museum’s hours before committing to a visit that is not essential to the walk.

If palaces already fill your schedule, the Archivo General de Indias offers a different perspective on Seville. The documents preserved here shed light on relations between Spain and its former overseas territories; the accessible exhibition spaces do not encompass all the archival storage areas. The building belongs to the same UNESCO World Heritage property as its neighbors. Start with the building’s exhibition spaces, then walk to the cathedral and the Alcázar, both next to the Archivo.

activities.text: In the narrow streets of the Barrio de Santa Cruz, shade almost becomes a route in itself. Small squares and tight passageways contrast with the expansive spaces of the cathedral and palaces, just nearby. Walk along looking at the courtyards visible from the street, staying on public paths. Save this loop for late in the day and head away from the busiest streets if you are looking for a break.

practical_info.tip: Self-guided walk; respect residential doorways and private entrances.

activities.text: Save the Parque de María Luisa for a walk without rushing to the next monument. Its tree-lined paths, pools, and pavilions extend your visit to the Plaza de España, on a different scale and with more shade. Its appeal lies in wandering among the gardens rather than checking off a list of sights. Bring water, choose a short loop, and save the large, exposed squares for cooler hours.

practical_info.tip: Flexible walking loop; shorten it if you are visiting several monuments on the same day.

map_keywords: Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre Jerez de la Frontera
Alcázar de Jerez de la Frontera
Catedral de Jerez de la Frontera

visits.text: An old mosque inside a fortress: the Alcázar de Jerez offers this unexpected combination. The baths and gardens round out your understanding of its Almohad heritage, offering far more than a simple tour of the walls. Choose the areas included in your ticket and check access to the camera obscura separately.

The exterior of the Catedral de Jerez de la Frontera also deserves your attention. It combines several architectural influences, while its bell tower stands apart from the main building—a detail easily missed if you head straight to the ticket office. First walk around the square in front, then check the sightseeing hours.

activities.text: Choose the Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre if a performance coincides with your visit. The work of the horses and riders takes the form of an equestrian ballet, with a schedule separate from tours of the facilities. Book the specific program you want and arrive before the announced start time.

practical_info.tip: A priority option for horse enthusiasts; choose it in place of another visit.

activities.text: If you prefer wine to the spectator stands, book a tour of the bodegas in Jerez. Sherry aging and the solera system give the tasting a clear theme that goes beyond the glass served at the end of the tour. Choose a short tour and plan who will drive after the tasting.

practical_info.tip: An alternative to the equestrian show; designate a driver who will not take part in the tasting.

visits.text: The waterfront light catches the dome of the Catedral de Cádiz. Its architecture comes into focus between the city’s closely packed facades and the open Atlantic; the contrast is part of the experience. Start in the square in front to take in the facade, then save the climb up the tower for a cooler morning.

The Torre Tavira offers a panorama you can also view in a darkened room. Its camera obscura projects views of Cádiz, providing a tangible way to understand the city and its watchtowers. Book a session in a language you understand and allow time for the terrace.

Finish at Playa de La Caleta, where the city almost directly meets the sand. Fortifications frame this small urban bay, and the boats recall a use of the shore beyond swimming. Come late in the day and check the tide before choosing a spot near the water.

activities.text: The colorful stalls of the Mercado Central de Cádiz offer a change of atmosphere after the monuments. The market and its Rincón Gastronómico let you sample coastal produce between visits. Come in the morning for the food stalls, then choose a tasting at the Rincón Gastronómico before getting back on the road.

practical_info.tip: Visit the market while it is operating; check the day and opening hours before you go.

map_keywords: Castillo de Vejer de la Frontera
Arco de las Monjas Vejer de la Frontera
Plaza de España Vejer de la Frontera

visits.text: Approaching through the narrow streets gives the Castillo de Vejer de la Frontera more context. Its elevated position explains the layout of the fortified town, and its gateway still reflects its Islamic heritage. Leave your car outside the walls and walk uphill through the narrow streets to the horseshoe-arched gateway.

A passage bears the name of its former neighbors: the Arco de las Monjas stands beside Vejer’s convent. The arch frames a view of the white houses, without requiring a lengthy visit. Find the viewpoint from the street and keep the passage clear when other walkers arrive.

The fountain’s colors enliven the white surroundings of Vejer’s Plaza de España. This square brings together facades and outdoor seating at the lower end of the old town, offering a change of atmosphere after the narrow streets around the castle. Settle into the shade for a short break before continuing toward Bolonia.

map_keywords: Conjunto Arqueológico de Baelo Claudia Tarifa

visits.text: At Baelo Claudia, the Roman city faces the Atlantic, with no modern urban backdrop around it. The forum, theater, and fish-salting facilities reveal different functions; garum connects the remains directly to fishing. Start early, bring water, and check which areas are accessible before your visit.

activities.text: Walk along Playa de Bolonia to extend your visit without feeling compelled to climb its dune. The shifting sand and pine forest reveal an evolving landscape right beside the Roman remains. Follow the marked access routes from the beach and turn back if a route is closed, without cutting through the pine forest.

practical_info.tip: Access to the dune trail may be partially closed; adjust your walk according to the trail markers.

map_keywords: Plaza del Cabildo Arcos de la Frontera
Basílica de Santa María Arcos de la Frontera

visits.text: The sheer drop suddenly comes into view at the edge of Plaza del Cabildo in Arcos de la Frontera. The overlook opens onto the Guadalete Valley, while the buildings around the square conceal its depth until the last moment. Walk into the center and avoid driving in without knowing the access routes.

An unfinished tower catches the eye at the Basílica de Santa María de la Asunción. Its side facade borders Plaza del Cabildo and already reveals several stages of construction. Take time to observe the exterior, then check opening hours if you would like to include the interior in this brief stop.

map_keywords: Castillo de Zahara de la Sierra
Puerto de las Palomas Zahara de la Sierra

visits.text: Climb to the Castillo de Zahara de la Sierra to see how the village fits into the surrounding terrain. The keep and the remains of the fortifications overlook the houses and the Zahara-El Gastor reservoir; the climb gives the panorama context. Wear shoes with good traction and skip the climb if heat or wind makes access difficult.

The stop matters more than the drive at Puerto de las Palomas. This pass connects Zahara de la Sierra to Grazalema along a mountain road, with views of the reservoir and surrounding terrain. Stop only in designated areas and adjust the crossing to the weather conditions.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via Puerto de las Palomas

visits.text: Grazalema’s white houses cluster at the foot of mountains that put the village’s scale into perspective. The narrow streets and squares make for a compact stop without turning this stage into a full day of hiking. Park away from the narrow passageways and bring an extra layer for changes in the weather in the sierra.

activities.text: If you would like to walk without devoting the day to the park, choose the Sendero de los Charcones. This route near Grazalema gives you access to the sierra landscape rather than the major regulated routes of the Pinsapar. Ask the tourist office about the day’s conditions and turn back according to the time you have available.

practical_info.tip: A short walk that can be adjusted; the major trails and their permits are not included.

visits.text: The gorge cuts sharply through the landscape beneath Ronda’s Puente Nuevo. The bridge connects the two parts of the city, but its significance becomes fully apparent when you view it from the overlooks. Take in the views from each side and check access routes before considering a descent into the Tajo.

Head down to the Baños Árabes de Ronda for a change of atmosphere after the overlooks. The cold, warm, and hot rooms reveal how the historic baths worked; openings in their vaulted ceilings create a distinctive light. Wear shoes suitable for steep slopes and check opening hours before leaving the center.

The architecture warrants a visit to the Plaza de Toros de Ronda, regardless of whether a performance is taking place. The galleries and arena offer a more intimate sense of scale than the sweeping landscapes of the Tajo; the museum provides context for the bullfighting tradition. Start with the galleries, then view the arena from the stands before walking to the Tajo overlooks.

map_keywords: Calle Cuevas del Sol Setenil de las Bodegas
Calle Cuevas de la Sombra Setenil de las Bodegas

visits.text: A roof of rock above a terrace: Calle Cuevas del Sol captures the essence of Setenil. The houses are built against natural overhangs rather than inside fully excavated caves, a detail that changes how you understand the village. Arrive before the crowds and keep passageways clear, even when taking a photograph.

Calle Cuevas de la Sombra takes the impression of a covered street even further. The rock extends over the walkway, very close to the river, explaining the contrast with its brighter neighbor. Walk over from Cuevas del Sol and leave your car outside this tightly confined area.

Standing stones become architecture at the Dólmenes de Antequera. Menga, Viera, and El Romeral display different forms; the UNESCO property also links the monuments to their natural landscape. Locate the entrances to the different sites and check opening hours, as they cannot all be visited through a single entrance.

activities.text: Choose a marked loop in the Torcal de Antequera to walk among the limestone formations. Erosion has carved stacks that sometimes look like built structures, although the terrain is natural. Plan for the drive from Antequera; if the upper parking lot is full, the final stretch is covered by shuttle or on foot from the lower parking lot. Start at the Centro de Visitantes Torcal Alto, then choose a marked loop and turn back if fog obscures the landmarks.

practical_info.tip: Allow for a driving detour; choose a short loop and cut back on the other visits planned for this half-day.

visits.text: Slowing down is the right way to experience the Palacios Nazaríes de la Alhambra. The courtyards, water features, and ornamentation reveal different perspectives just a few steps apart; tightly framed photographs do little to convey this sequence. Entry is tied to a specific time slot, separate from the overall time spent in the monumental complex. Buy tickets on the official website, check which documents are required, and allow extra time before entering the palaces, even if you are already on-site.

The sound of water accompanies your walk through the Generalife, above Granada. The gardens and courtyards of this residence complement the Alhambra palaces, with a more open relationship to the plantings and landscape. They are not a detour to improvise at the last minute if your ticket already sets out your admission arrangements. Check the included route and plan this visit around your palace time slot, allowing time to get between sites.

The Mirador de San Nicolás brings the Alhambra and the hills behind the city into a single view. The vista explains its popularity, but the square can become crowded when everyone seeks the same shot at sunset. The neighborhood is still residential, and its streets offer other perspectives too. Come earlier if you want to take in the view peacefully, then continue on foot without blocking residents’ entrances or the narrow streets leading to the square.

A large Renaissance cathedral near the old narrow streets: the Catedral de Granada brings a change of pace. Its light-filled spaces and the arrangement of its chapels offer a different way to understand the city from the Nasrid palaces. The neighboring Capilla Real is a separate visit; save the Albaicín for another half-day.

If you want to understand Granada’s political transition, add the Capilla Real de Granada. The tombs of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon put faces to this chapter of history, in a space whose scale contrasts with the neighboring cathedral. The collections add context to the tombs when the rooms are accessible. Pair the chapel with the neighboring cathedral, reaching both in a single walk from the downtown streets instead of making a round trip to the Alhambra.

activities.text: Explore the Albaicín by linking its small squares rather than heading only for an overlook. Houses with gardens, known as cármenes, are part of the neighborhood’s identity, but an open door does not make them public spaces. The slopes and cobblestones also call for a different pace than downtown. Wear good shoes, bring water, and choose a loop that gradually descends toward the city, avoiding repeated climbs between viewpoints.

practical_info.tip: Self-guided walk; adjust the length to account for the slopes and respect private entrances to the cármenes.

activities.text: If you want to see flamenco, Sacromonte is an option to consider during your stay in Granada. The neighborhood is associated with cave dwellings and performance venues, whose programs and arrangements vary. Compare the duration and what the ticket includes before booking; also plan your return to your accommodation, since an evening out changes the pace of the next day’s visits.

practical_info.tip: Compare show packages and arrange your return trip before booking.

map_keywords: Fuente del Rey Priego de Córdoba
Barrio de la Villa Priego de Córdoba

visits.text: The sound of water announces the Fuente del Rey before its sculptures come into view. Its 139 jets surround the pools, with an abundance of faces and decorative details: it is better to study a few figures than try to count everything. Use this brief stop as a break and check for any access restrictions.

The Barrio de la Villa draws Priego de Córdoba into narrow streets lined with white buildings and cobbled passageways. The Balcón del Adarve then opens up views of the surrounding terrain, offering a breathing space at the edge of the neighborhood. Explore on foot after parking outside the neighborhood, and keep residential entrances clear during your stops.

map_keywords: Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos Córdoba

visits.text: A cathedral in the middle of a former mosque: the Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba makes you examine the site’s layers. The rows of arches and the central Christian space create different perspectives, making this a monument that cannot be understood from a single vantage point. The contrast speaks for itself, without a stream of figures about the columns. Book a cultural visit on the official website, check worship times, and allow plenty of time to explore the areas open to visitors.

Allow time for the gardens of the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos after the more confined spaces of downtown. The pools and plantings are part of the route, while the accessible rooms and towers offer another way to understand the fortress. Access may vary depending on construction work and visiting conditions. Plan to see the gardens during the first hours after opening and bring water, especially if you continue afterward through the streets of the Judería.

A small room is enough to bring a change of scale at the Sinagoga de Córdoba. In the narrow streets of the Judería, its decoration preserves another trace of the city’s religious history, distinct from the large neighboring complexes. The visit is short, but the inscriptions and details reward unhurried attention. Include the synagogue in your walk through the Judería and examine the wall inscriptions before heading back toward the mosque-cathedral.

Medina Azahara is worth the trip for its landscape as much as its remains. The terraces of this palatial city, commissioned by Abd al-Rahman III, place caliphal power beyond Córdoba’s narrow streets; preservation and access vary across the site. The interpretation center helps you understand the structures that have disappeared. Start at the interpretation center, then head to the ruins; allow for the return to Córdoba within the same sightseeing window.

The Puente Romano de Córdoba draws your attention above all to the two riverbanks. From the pedestrian crossing, the silhouette of the Mezquita-Catedral takes its place in the Guadalquivir landscape, while the opposite bank offers a different perspective on the city. The bridge has undergone changes throughout its history: its name does not tell the whole story of what you see. Come as the light fades, then spend some time on the riverbank instead of immediately crossing back.

activities.text: If you want to walk between two reserved visits, the Judería de Córdoba offers a compact loop. Its narrow streets connect small squares and buildings whose patios are sometimes visible, but the patio festival and regular opening arrangements follow different rules. Choose patios with organized visits and leave private courtyards to their residents. Set out on foot from the mosque-cathedral area, enjoy the shade, and respect private entrances.

practical_info.tip: Private patios are not included; check organized visits and the festival calendar separately.

map_keywords: Alcázar de la Puerta de Sevilla Carmona

visits.text: Climb into the Alcázar de la Puerta de Sevilla to understand Carmona from its gateway. The terraces overlook the city and farmland, while alterations to the fortification tell the story of successive occupations. Leave your car outside the old town, enter through the Puerta de Sevilla, and continue on foot through the narrow streets after visiting the fortress.

The city of the dead begins beyond Carmona’s narrow streets, at the Necrópolis Romana. The burial chambers and preserved remains shift the focus from panoramic views to ancient practices; some spaces can only be viewed from outside. Start with the open-air sections during the cooler hours, then view the burial chambers from the designated paths.

Beneath the castle hill, another Aracena awaits in the Gruta de las Maravillas. The pools and mineral formations completely transform the landscape, just a few steps from the village above. Book a guided tour, bring a light layer, and check the photography rules before descending.

The climb to the Castillo de Aracena helps place the cave in its landscape. Visiting the summit and the fortified ruins offers views of the houses and hills, rather than a fully furnished castle. Walk up to the summit after visiting the cave beneath the same hill.

The Museo del Jamón de Aracena places ham in the context of the surrounding landscape. The exhibits cover livestock farming, the dehesa, and ham production. Combine this museum and the castle with the Aracena tourist card, then save the tasting for the shops in the center.

The walls of the Castelo de Serpa come into view before the narrow streets of the center. The Moura and Beja gates provide landmarks along the fortifications, while the houses extend the route inside. Enter through the Porta de Moura or the Porta de Beja, then walk up to the upper quarter before the hottest hours.

You will follow the arches of the Aqueduto de Serpa from outside the city walls. Their proximity to the palace of the Counts of Ficalho shows how defense, housing, and water supply overlapped here. Find an unobstructed view from a public space and keep this visit short before continuing to Monsaraz.

activities.text: For a food break, try Queijo Serpa DOP in the center of Serpa. This sheep’s milk cheese is made using a thistle infusion to curdle the milk: a detail to ask about during the tasting. Choose a small portion and keep your purchases chilled.

practical_info.tip: Choose a short tasting and plan a way to keep perishable products chilled.

visits.text: The landscape makes the climb to the Castelo de Monsaraz, above the countryside, worthwhile. From the accessible areas, the walls frame Alqueva and the countryside, offering a different sense of scale from the narrow streets. Save the end of the day for the areas around the walls, then head back down through the narrow streets to the parking areas outside.

The Rua Direita in Monsaraz connects white facades in a village explored on foot. Views toward the walls and countryside emerge along the small streets, without the need for a long guided tour. Leave your car in the parking areas outside and wear shoes suitable for cobblestones.

A Roman temple that became a municipal butcher shop: the Templo Romano de Évora has had an unexpected history. Its columns now rise above the Largo do Conde de Vila Flor, but its later uses also help explain its preservation. Its common name, the Temple of Diana, does not establish that it was dedicated to that deity. Walk around it from the public space, look at the podium, and choose side lighting to better appreciate its forms.

In the Capela dos Ossos, your eye shifts between the patterns and the material used to make them. The bones incorporated into the decoration of this chapel in the Igreja de São Francisco serve as a reminder of life’s fragility, in a space smaller than photographs suggest. Check access to the church and the chapel separately. Decide whether to visit based on your comfort level and remain discreet throughout the religious complex.

You will climb toward the Sé de Évora to connect the Roman temple with the city’s medieval skyline. The cathedral, cloister, and any access to elevated areas are not all included in every admission option, so the route you choose shapes the experience. When open, the terraces help you understand the center as a whole. Choose the option that covers the spaces you want to see, then save the climb to the terrace for the cooler hours between two visits in the center.

If road access allows, the Cromeleque dos Almendres offers a counterpoint to the center of Évora. The standing stones can be appreciated in an open landscape; their appeal lies as much in their arrangement as in the absence of surrounding buildings. This excursion involves a round trip outside the city and should not be treated as a stop near the cathedral. Plan the round trip to Almendres from Évora as a single excursion before continuing toward Beja.

activities.text: The Praça do Giraldo provides a useful reference point for walking through Évora. The arcades, shopping streets, and small squares let you connect the major monuments without constantly returning to your car. It is also a way to observe the facades and everyday life between indoor visits. Start from the square, choose a compact loop, and allow for a break in the shade, keeping the hottest hours in the Alentejo in mind.

practical_info.tip: Self-guided walk through the historic center; the excursion to Almendres remains optional.

map_keywords: Museu Regional Rainha D. Leonor Beja

visits.text: Gaining elevation at the Castelo de Beja adds perspective to this stop on the plain. Its keep and ramparts offer a different view of the city, even though not all areas are accessible on every visit. Save the climb to the keep for the cool morning hours and walk around the ramparts before heading back down into town.

A former convent accounts for the outline of the Museu Regional Rainha D. Leonor. Access to its collections and historic spaces depends on the renovation and reopening schedule, however: keep an exterior stop on your itinerary during a closure. View the facade of the Convento da Conceição from the public space as you head down from the castle toward the center.

You will climb to the Castelo de Mértola to place the village in the context of its rivers and slopes. The keep and fortified ruins overlook the houses, while the Guadiana explains the importance of this location. Wear shoes suitable for steps and save the climb for the cooler hours.

A church here preserves traces of a mosque: the Igreja Matriz de Mértola tells the story of its transformation in stone. The horseshoe arches and mihrab reveal the building’s former use without the need for a long list of dates. Enter outside service times, then look for the horseshoe arches and mihrab while remaining discreet in this place of worship.

The Islamic art section of the Museu de Mértola complements what the church reveals. Its objects and archaeological finds tell the story of life in the town, beyond its ramparts and panoramic views. Combine this section and the church in the same route, rather than making repeated trips between the museum’s different spaces.

activities.text: Light glides along the Guadiana in Mértola, making the houses stand out against the hillside. A walk through the public spaces near the river offers another perspective on the town, which was once connected to river trade. Choose a short route, avoid undeveloped riverbanks, and head back uphill before the hottest hours.

practical_info.tip: Adjust the walk to suit you using public access routes; bring water for the climb back up.

map_keywords: Forte de São Clemente Vila Nova de Milfontes

visits.text: The estuary helps put the Forte de São Clemente in context, with the Mira in the background. This fortification in Vila Nova de Milfontes protected the entrance against attacks from the sea; view its silhouette from the waterfront. Observe the facades from public spaces and continue toward the water’s edge.

Take a detour to Cabo Sardão to view the coast from its cliffs. The lighthouse provides a landmark in an open landscape that differs from the Milfontes estuary; this visit involves traveling outside the village. Stay behind the barriers and adjust your walk to the wind, without approaching the edge to take photos.

activities.text: For a quiet walk, walk along Praia da Franquia beside the estuary. The ocean’s proximity does not eliminate the effects of the tides or the Mira’s currents; a walk does not require a swim. Walk from the waterfront to the beach, then save the detour to Cabo Sardão for the next driving leg.

practical_info.tip: Walk along the beach and public access routes; swim only when conditions permit it.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Cabo Sardão, optional coastal detour

visits.text: Two bodies of water meet at Praia de Odeceixe: the Seixe River and the Atlantic shape different shores. The landscape changes with the tide; treat the river and the oceanfront as two distinct viewpoints. Come at low tide to observe the pools formed in the sand and stay on the designated access routes near the river.

The Moinho de Odeceixe offers a view of the village before you reach the beach. From its hill, the white houses and the Seixe Valley reveal the transition from the interior to the coast. Walk up through the village’s narrow streets for the panorama, then save the trip to the beach for the next part of your stop.

The remains of a fortress reveal the contours of the landscape at Castelo de Aljezur. The walls overlook the old town and its valley, while the houses follow the slopes rather than a regular layout. Walk up from an authorized parking area and adjust your visit to the access routes that are open and the condition of the steps.

Head to the ruins of the Fortaleza da Arrifana to view the bay from above. Praia da Arrifana nestles beneath the cliffs, with houses following the slope: the detour complements your visit to Aljezur. Stay in safe areas and avoid exposed ledges when the wind picks up.

The wind gives you a sense of the promontory’s scale at the Fortaleza de Sagres. The open spaces, church, and traces of former installations matter as much as the walls; the visit mainly involves walking outdoors. Bring a windproof layer, check which access routes are open that day, and stay well away from unprotected edges.

The view alone justifies the detour to Cabo de São Vicente, even without visiting its lighthouse. The cliffs and the Atlantic dominate the landscape, while the proximity to Sagres lets you compare two different promontories. Include the cape as a complement to the fortress, then follow the designated paths around the lighthouse wearing a windbreaker.

Follow the designated access routes at Ponta da Piedade for changing perspectives on the cliffs. You can observe the arches and cavities from above without taking a boat trip; some stairways lead farther down. Choose your route according to the conditions, bring water, and stay on authorized paths.

The Museu de Lagos combines its collections with the Igreja de Santo António in the historic center. The church interior is part of the museum route, so tickets and opening hours matter more than they would for simply entering a place of worship. Choose the museum route that includes the Igreja de Santo António, then continue your walk through the historic center.

activities.text: The stairway at Praia do Camilo gradually reveals a small cove between the cliffs. The access route is part of the experience, but it also means climbing back up after your break; this compact beach fills up quickly. Go down only if your mobility allows it, and avoid settling at the base of the cliff faces.

practical_info.tip: Optional beach break; plan for the climb back up and heed the cliff hazard signs.

map_keywords: Percurso dos Sete Vales Suspensos Lagoa

visits.text: It is best to start at the top at Praia da Marinha. The cliffs frame the beach and help you understand the coastal terrain before deciding whether to descend; you do not need to reach every stretch of sand to enjoy the view. Come early and respect the barriers and signs along the cliff faces.

activities.text: Book an authorized excursion to Algar de Benagil if sea conditions allow. The opening at the top lights the interior, but the rules prohibit swimming into the cave and landing on the sand. Choose a regulated operator and confirm the refund terms for weather-related cancellations.

practical_info.tip: Access is regulated: no swimming or landing; kayaking is allowed only on an authorized guided tour.

activities.text: If you prefer walking, choose a section of the Percurso dos Sete Vales Suspensos. The trail follows the cliffs between the Praia da Marinha and Vale de Centeanes areas; the full loop is beyond the scope of this brief stop. Bring water, stay on the marked trail, and turn back according to your schedule.

practical_info.tip: An alternative to the boat trip: a short walk returning to the same starting point, excluding the full route.

visits.text: One last gateway to finish the loop: the Arco da Vila marks the entrance to Faro’s old town. Its passage connects the marina area to the historic center without requiring another full visit. Keep this stop optional and prioritize leaving enough time to return the car and reach your departure point.

seo.h1_title: Algarve, Andalusia, and Alentejo Road Trip in 20 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: This 20-day loop starts in Faro, crosses Andalusia, then returns to Portugal through Alentejo and the Vicentine Coast. It connects Seville, Granada, and Córdoba with white villages, the Roman remains of Baelo Claudia, and the cliffs of the Algarve. Choose sea activities and longer excursions according to your pace and access conditions.
seo.seo_hook: Set out from Faro for 20 days through the Algarve, Seville, Granada, Córdoba, and Alentejo, with white villages, Atlantic cliffs, and historic sites.
featured_list: Faro and Tavira: historic towns on the shores of Ria Formosa.
Seville and Granada: palaces, gardens, and old neighborhoods.
Córdoba: the Mezquita-Catedral and an excursion to Medina Azahara.
Évora and Mértola: Roman, medieval, and Islamic heritage.
Sagres, Lagos, and Benagil: headlands, cliffs, and regulated access by sea.
